<reflection>
- The third experiment (high substrate, high catalyst) successfully widened the gap between the top candidates. By pushing the catalyst primarily into the substrate-bound state (catS), M19 (NLL -58.0) significantly outperformed M18 (NLL -51.5). The first-order deactivation models (M11, M16) fell much further behind.
- My aim was achieved: we have isolated M19 and M18 as the only highly plausible mechanisms, both of which involve second-order catalyst deactivation, but with different species dependencies.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To definitively confirm the second-order nature of the deactivation and to distinguish the subtle dynamic differences between M19 (cat + catS => inactive) and M18 (2catS => inactive), we should lower the initial catalyst concentration to 0.05 and use a moderate substrate concentration of 1.0.
1. **Second-order vs. First-order:** By reducing the catalyst concentration by a factor of 2 to 4 compared to previous runs, any second-order deactivation (M18, M19) will drop by a factor of 4 to 16, whereas first-order deactivation (M11, M16) would only drop linearly. If M18/M19 are correct, the catalyst will survive much longer and achieve a higher turnover number than in previous experiments, definitively ruling out the remaining first-order models.
2. **M19 vs. M18 Dynamics:** With a moderate substrate concentration, the reaction will progress and substrate will deplete, causing the system to transition from a high [catS] state to a high free [cat] state. 
   - For M18, the deactivation rate ($\propto$ [catS]^2) will monotonically decrease as the substrate is consumed.
   - For M19, the deactivation rate ($\propto$ [cat][catS]) will actually peak mid-reaction when [cat] $\approx$ [catS] (i.e., when substrate concentration approaches the Michaelis constant, Km). 
This difference in the timing of maximum deactivation will produce distinct curvature in the product formation profile, allowing us to confidently isolate the true mechanism.
</hypothesis>
